title: The three hours
hookLine: some churches keep noon to three on Good Friday with his seven last words

cards: "Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land unto the ninth hour." That's Matthew, in the King James Bible, describing the afternoon of the crucifixion.
The sixth hour to the ninth: on our clocks, around noon to three. On Good Friday, some churches keep exactly those hours. The doors stay open.
People come in on a lunch break and leave again, or sit through the whole afternoon. There are readings, a few hymns, and long stretches of silence.
And running through it, one at a time, are the things Jesus said from the cross. Today, the three hours.

teach.b: No single Gospel has all seven sayings. Tradition gathers them from the four Gospels and sets them in an order. In Luke, Jesus says, "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do."
To a criminal crucified beside him, who asks to be remembered: "To day shalt thou be with me in paradise."
In John, he looks down at his mother and his friend: "Woman, behold thy son!" and to the friend, "Behold thy mother!"
Then the cry Matthew and Mark both keep: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" the first line of Psalm 22. Back in John: "I thirst." Then: "It is finished."
And Luke's last: "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit." Now look at the shape.
The first three words are for other people: the ones killing him, a stranger dying next to him, his mother. In that much pain, he's still giving things away.

teach.h: THEN THE CRY OF BEING FORSAKEN.
teach.b: Then the dark center, the cry of being forsaken, prayed in the words of a psalm.
Then the body: thirst. Then the work done. Then trust.

Christians hear different things in the sayings, and churches that keep the three hours may preach on each in turn. But the order alone teaches something: from others, through abandonment, to rest in God's hands.
The three hours give each word room, so none gets rushed.

how: Some churches hold a Good Friday service from noon to three, with readings, hymns, silence and short meditations on each of the seven sayings of Jesus from the cross; people may stay for part or all of it.

o: the day of the cross, kept with silence and readings
the Friday a church gives food to the poor
the Friday before Lent, when the fast begins

games.q: where each word comes from — tap the pairs.
p: the sixth hour to the ninth

s: one Gospel records all seven words
they're gathered from the four. Luke has three, John has three, and Matthew and Mark share the cry.
in John, Jesus gives his mother and his friend to each other from the cross
woman, behold thy son! and to the friend, behold thy mother!
in the usual order, the first words are about his own pain
the first three are for others: his killers, a criminal beside him, his mother.

games.q: you're the criminal crucified beside Jesus. the man on the other side is mocking him. what do you say?
o: Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.
games.why: he asks to be remembered, and Jesus answers: "to day shalt thou be with me in paradise."

practice: Read the seven words slowly, a breath between each: forgive them, today in paradise, behold thy son, behold thy mother, why hast thou forsaken me, I thirst, it is finished, into thy hands.
Go back to whichever one caught on something and stay with it, and if you pray, let it become your prayer; if not, just let it sit with you.

wordCard.voice: Good Friday, the day Christians keep noon to three with silence, readings, and the seven words from the cross.

orig.note: Greek: it is finished — one word in John 19:30.

carryVoice: Your line: the seven words. Each one given room. Go gently today, and I'll see you tomorrow.
